title: A study to investigate the use of a proprietary wound dressing to reduce ankle swelling to quicken time to surgery
official: A randomised pilot study to determine the time to surgery when using a polymeric dressing for the alleviation of swelling prior to fixation of an ankle fracture
summary:
Background and study aims 
The aim is to determine whether a proprietary dressing used for the treatment of injuries and known to reduce swelling can be used to ensure that patients, suffering an ankle fracture, are ready for surgery on day 7. This would enable patients to be sent home instead of kept on a ward, which could release up to 90,000 bed days per years as well as making the whole process more efficient.

Who can participate? 
Patients aged 18 to 100 years presenting to A&E in the Royal Stoke University Hospital with an unstable ankle fracture

What does the study involve? 
Patients will be randomly allocated into two groups. Group 1, the active group, will have the proprietary dressing in addition to any temporary fixation. Those in Group 2 are the control and have not additional dressing. Once the patient is approved for surgery their participation in the study is complete.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
The potential benefit is having an ankle fracture treated earlier than normal (group 1). As the dressing is commonly used in orthopaedics, dermatology and other clinical settings there are no perceived risks from participating.

Where is the study run from? 
Royal Stoke University Hospital (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
November 2026 to May 2027

Who is funding the study? 
Investigator initiated and funded

Who is the main contact? 
Peter J Ogrodnik, p.ogrodnik@keele.ac.uk
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Aged 18 to 100 years
2. Lower leg distal fracture requiring surgical intervention that is delayed due to oedema
Exclusion criteria:
1. Under the age of 18 years
2. Over the age of 100 years
3. Not skeletally mature
4. Patients presenting poly-trauma
5. Those whose definitive fixation is not delayed due to excessive oedema
6. Those unable to give informed consent
7. Patients on regular anti-inflammatories (e.g. taken daily for the previous 7 days)
8. On medication that precludes this procedure, e.g. anti-coagulants
